public_rationale: The claim is near-universal: for essentially everything LLMs talk about, nearly any generalization breaks easily under distribution shift. Studies from before the post back it in places. Shi et al. (Jan 2023) found LLM math accuracy 'dramatically decreased' when irrelevant sentences were added. Razeghi et al. (2022) found accuracy depended strongly on how often terms appeared in pretraining. But there are partial counterexamples. Minerva reached over 80% accuracy on 10-digit addition, generalizing well beyond common examples, though accuracy fell to about 20% at 18 digits. All of this evidence is narrow, mostly arithmetic. Nothing I found tests the claim's universal scope, and 'easily broken' has no threshold. The evidence fits brittleness in specific cases but cannot confirm or refute 'nearly any' generalization across 'essentially everything'.
limitations: Evidence is concentrated in math and arithmetic.
The outcome turns on how much brittleness counts as 'nearly any' and 'easily'.

statement.excerpt: The same goes for essentially everything an LLMs talks about; there is a degree of generalization to similar examples, but distribution shift is hard (the crux of my own work going back to 1998), and nearly any generalization can be easily broken.

our_interpretation: Plain reading: across nearly all domains, LLMs of the time generalize to inputs similar to their training data, but small or moderate changes to inputs (distribution shift) easily break that generalization.
Target period: LLMs as studied from 2022-01 to the post date (2023-03-12). This is my choice, because the claim describes a present state without naming a period.
criteria.support_condition: Robustness and distribution-shift studies of contemporary LLMs show, across many domains, that performance collapses under small or modest input changes, with few robust exceptions.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Studies of contemporary LLMs show robust generalization under distribution shift in a broad range of domains, so 'nearly any' generalization does not break easily.

evidence.explanation: Consistent with generalization limited to cases like the training data, but limited to numerical tasks in GPT-style models trained on the Pile.

evidence.explanation: Minerva held over 80% accuracy on 10-digit addition, far from typical training examples. That is generalization that did not break easily, though it fell off at 18 digits.
